sections.title: Reading the BBQ-and-case brief as a production contract

questions.question: According to the theory, the approved project brief should be treated as what?
questions.feedback: The theory describes the approved project brief as a production contract because it defines required outcomes, limits and the evidence that must be collected.

questions.question: Before practical work begins, what should students create from the brief, drawings and evidence list?
questions.feedback: Translating the brief, drawings and evidence list into a folio checklist helps separate required actions from assumptions before production starts.

questions.question: Which example is identified as a project requirement?
options: An identified function required by the brief
An unverified idea added during production
questions.feedback: The theory states that a project requirement is a condition that must be met, such as an identified function, specified evidence or a teacher-controlled feature.

questions.question: What should a student do if an important project detail is unclear?
options: Confirm the detail with the teacher
questions.feedback: The theory explains that unclear details should be confirmed with the teacher rather than being invented by the student.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a student preference?
options: It can override required processes if practical
It may be considered only when the brief allows flexibility
questions.feedback: Preferences are only acceptable where the brief allows flexibility and cannot override drawings, required processes or approval points.

questions.question: What does planning the BBQ and case as a connected product system involve?
options: Identifying shared requirements, interfaces and evidence
Assuming both products use the same construction
questions.feedback: The theory says the products should be planned together by identifying shared requirements, interfaces and evidence, not by guessing construction details.

questions.question: A student wants to change a teacher-controlled feature because they think it will work better. Based on the theory, what is the correct response?
options: Proceed if the change seems reasonable
Treat the feature as fixed unless the teacher approves a change
Replace the feature with a personal preference
questions.feedback: Authorised requirements remain fixed unless the teacher approves a change. Personal preferences cannot override compulsory project conditions.

questions.question: How does a clear checklist support quality control?
options: By replacing the need for evidence
By showing that production followed the approved brief
By allowing project requirements to change during production
questions.feedback: A checklist provides a record that practical work developed from the approved brief rather than from unverified personal interpretation.

questions.question: Which planning approach best matches the key takeaways?
options: Mix compulsory conditions and personal preferences in one list
Ignore links between the BBQ and case until evaluation
Record allowable preferences separately from compulsory conditions
questions.feedback: Keeping allowable preferences separate from compulsory conditions helps ensure required project expectations remain clear and traceable.

questions.question: According to the source boundary, where should unresolved project-specific details come from?
options: The teacher-issued project documents and demonstrations
General assumptions based on similar projects
questions.feedback: The source boundary states that unresolved project-specific details are controlled by the teacher-issued project brief, drawings, SOPs, WMS template and demonstrations.

sections.title: From hazard review to a task-specific WMS

questions.question: What is the main purpose of hazard identification during a task?
options: To recognise what could cause harm
To approve the use of equipment
To describe the operating steps for a machine
questions.feedback: Hazard identification focuses on recognising sources of potential harm before work begins. It does not approve equipment use or replace operating procedures.

questions.question: According to the theory, what is the primary role of an SOP?
options: To combine planning, permissions and hold points for a project
To provide the approved operating requirements for a particular tool, machine or process
To record evidence that production has been completed
questions.feedback: An SOP defines the approved operating requirements for a specific tool, machine or process. It has a different purpose from a WMS.

questions.question: Which combination best describes what a Year 10 Work Method Statement (WMS) records?
options: Task sequence, hazards, controls, permission requirements and hold points
Only a list of general workshop hazards
Only the completed evidence collected after production
questions.feedback: A WMS organises the planned work into stages and records the task, hazards, controls, permission requirements and hold points for each stage.

questions.question: Why does the theory recommend planning safety decisions before practical work begins?
options: To reduce the need for supervision
To avoid making hurried safety decisions during production
To replace the need for current demonstrations
questions.feedback: Planning ahead allows hazards, controls and checks to be considered before work starts instead of relying on rushed decisions during production.

questions.question: A project includes cutting, drilling, machining, joining and finishing. What does the WMS help students identify?
options: Which different SOPs or demonstrations apply at different stages
Which project dimensions should be changed
Which assessment result will be awarded
questions.feedback: The WMS links each stage of work with the relevant SOPs or demonstrations that apply to that part of the production process.

questions.question: According to the theory, why do lathe operations require particular attention in the WMS?
options: Because lathe work is exempt from normal planning
Because lathe operations are specifically identified as requiring a WMS
Because lathe work never requires supervision
questions.feedback: The theory states that lathe operations require particular attention because the authorised scope specifically requires a WMS for this work.

questions.question: A student finishes writing a complete WMS. What does the theory say this document provides?
options: Automatic permission to begin using equipment
Evidence that planning has been completed
questions.feedback: A completed WMS is evidence of planning. It does not authorise equipment use or replace demonstrations, supervision or approved procedures.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes hazard reviews from SOPs?
options: Hazard reviews identify risks, while SOPs define approved procedures
Hazard reviews replace SOPs once production starts
Hazard reviews and SOPs have exactly the same purpose
questions.feedback: Hazard reviews focus on recognising risks, while SOPs specify the approved way to operate a particular tool, machine or process.

questions.question: Which situation best demonstrates the purpose of a hold point in a WMS?
options: Skipping directly to the next stage once work feels complete
Stopping work at a planned point for checking or teacher authorisation
Recording the final project evaluation after production
questions.feedback: A hold point is a planned stage where work stops so required checks or teacher authorisation can occur before continuing.

questions.question: According to the source boundary, where do unresolved task-specific safety and operating details come from?
options: The current teacher-issued SOPs, WMS template and demonstrations
questions.feedback: The source boundary states that unresolved task-specific safety and operating details are controlled by the current teacher-issued SOPs, WMS template and demonstrations.

sections.title: Inputs, processes and outputs as a planning model

questions.question: According to the input–process–output model, which item is an input?
questions.feedback: Inputs are the resources needed before work begins, such as approved materials, drawings, information, equipment, time and teacher instructions. Completed components and folio evidence are outputs.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a process in the input–process–output model?
options: To transform inputs into products and evidence
To record only the finished project
questions.feedback: Processes are the controlled transformations applied to inputs. They produce both physical work and evidence recorded throughout production.

questions.question: A student creates a flowchart that simply lists tasks from top to bottom without showing connections or checks. Based on the theory, what is missing?
options: The way stages connect through inputs, changes, checks and evidence
questions.feedback: The theory explains that a production flowchart should show how stages connect, including what enters each stage, what changes, what is checked and what evidence is recorded, rather than being only a task list.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a quality hold point?
options: To pause production so quality or approval can be confirmed
To increase the number of production stages
questions.feedback: A quality hold point deliberately pauses production so accuracy, fit, alignment, completeness or approval can be checked before work continues.

questions.question: If a quality check identifies a problem, what does the feedback loop show should happen?
options: Continue to the next stage anyway
Return to an earlier stage for correction or further planning
questions.feedback: A feedback loop directs the process back to an earlier stage so corrections, adjustments or additional planning can occur before production continues.

questions.question: Which group contains only examples of inputs mentioned in the theory?
options: Approved materials, drawings and teacher instructions
Completed components, checked surfaces and folio evidence
Assembled work, completed components and checked surfaces
questions.feedback: Inputs include approved materials, drawings, measurements, information, equipment, time and teacher instructions. The other options list outputs.

questions.question: Why does the theory describe the flowchart as a practical control document?
options: Because it helps coordinate resources, sequence work, document quality and prevent unnoticed errors moving forward
Because it contains all unresolved project-specific details
questions.feedback: The flowchart supports production by coordinating resources, sequencing work, documenting quality and reducing the chance of carrying errors into later stages.

questions.question: Which statement best describes an output in this planning model?
options: A resource that controls the exact production sequence
Completed work or evidence produced during production
questions.feedback: Outputs include completed components, assembled work, checked surfaces and folio evidence created throughout the production process.

questions.question: According to the source boundary, where do the exact production sequence and unresolved project-specific details come from?
options: The teacher-issued production plan, drawings and demonstrations
questions.feedback: The source boundary states that the teacher-issued production plan, drawings and demonstrations control the exact sequence and any unresolved project-specific details.

questions.question: What should each stage of the BBQ and case production flowchart identify before work moves forward?
options: Only the name of the task
What enters the process, what changes, what must be checked and what evidence should be recorded
questions.feedback: Each stage should identify its inputs, the transformation taking place, the required quality checks and the evidence to record before progressing to the next stage.

sections.title: Selecting stock form by function and manufacture

questions.question: According to the theory, selecting metal stock involves choosing what?
options: A form suited to function and manufacture
questions.feedback: Choosing stock includes selecting a form that supports both the component's purpose and its manufacturing requirements.

questions.question: Where must the exact stock grades and sizes be confirmed?
options: The issued drawing and cutting information
questions.feedback: The theory states that exact grades and sizes come from the issued drawing and cutting information.

questions.question: Which factor should be considered when judging a suitable stock form?
questions.feedback: Joining access affects whether components can be assembled effectively using the approved manufacturing approach.

questions.question: Why should students identify usable offcuts before production?
options: To reduce unnecessary waste through planning
questions.feedback: Planning layouts and identifying usable offcuts improves efficiency without altering the authorised specification.

questions.question: Which statement best matches the theory about manufacturing efficiency?
options: Ignore offcuts if enough stock is available
questions.feedback: Efficiency comes from thoughtful planning, quantity checks and layout decisions rather than changing approved specifications.

questions.question: What should guide unresolved stock specifications and project details?
options: Teacher-issued drawings, cutting information and demonstrations
questions.feedback: The source boundary assigns unresolved stock specifications and project-specific details to teacher-issued project information.

questions.question: A stock form seems suitable but blocks joining access. What does the theory suggest?
options: Reassess the stock form because manufacture is affected
Use it anyway because function matters most
Ignore joining access if waste is low
questions.feedback: A suitable selection must support both function and practical manufacture, including adequate joining access.

questions.question: Which combination best reflects the key considerations when selecting stock form?
questions.feedback: The key takeaway emphasises balancing function, material properties and manufacturing requirements during selection.

questions.question: Which condition could make an otherwise suitable stock form impractical?
questions.feedback: The theory explains that excessive waste can make an otherwise suitable stock form impractical.

questions.question: Why should available workshop processes be considered during stock selection?
options: To ensure the stock can be processed accurately
questions.feedback: Available processes must be capable of accurately shaping, cutting, drilling or assembling the selected stock form.

sections.title: Turning drawings into freehand sketches and a spreadsheet cutting list

questions.question: What should students do before marking or cutting material?
options: Convert drawings into organised production information
questions.feedback: Production information should be organised from verified drawings before any material is marked or cut.

questions.question: Why should information be cross-checked across different drawing views?
options: Different views can reveal different component features
Each view uses different measurement units
One view always contains incorrect information
questions.feedback: Cross-checking views combines their information and reduces the risk of overlooking an important feature.

questions.question: What is the correct response when data appears to be missing from a drawing?
questions.feedback: Missing data must not be invented or measured from the image; teacher clarification controls unresolved information.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a freehand component sketch?
options: Show how the component has been interpreted
questions.feedback: A freehand sketch demonstrates understanding of general form, important features and relationships between drawing views.

questions.question: Which detail is appropriate to include on a freehand sketch?
options: Brief annotations linked to verified dimensions or notes
Dimensions measured from the printed image
questions.feedback: Brief annotations can identify where confirmed drawing dimensions or notes apply without replacing the formal drawing.

questions.question: Which cutting-list entry should remain blank?
questions.feedback: Unconfirmed quantities, allowances and tolerances must remain blank until authorised information or teacher clarification is provided.

questions.question: Which spreadsheet practice best supports accurate production information?
options: Mixing units to match stock types
Using consistent units for every entry
questions.feedback: Consistent units help entries match written drawing information and reduce avoidable interpretation errors during production.

questions.question: What should be recorded when the drawing provides revision information?
options: The current revision or issue date
questions.feedback: Recording the supplied revision or issue date helps ensure the cutting list uses the current authorised information.

questions.question: When should the spreadsheet cutting list be updated?
options: Whenever a student notices a possible improvement
After material has already been cut
When an authorised drawing change occurs
questions.feedback: The spreadsheet must reflect authorised changes so outdated information does not guide later production decisions.

questions.question: What final check should occur before practical work begins?
options: Compare the cutting list only with stock available
Cross-check drawings, sketches, cutting list and teacher clarification
Measure every drawing view with a ruler
questions.feedback: Cross-checking all verified sources prevents an early information error from becoming wasted material during production.

sections.title: Datums, orientation and quality gates for rails and end caps

questions.question: What is a datum used for during marking out?
options: An agreed reference edge, face or point
questions.feedback: Using one agreed reference helps measurements stay consistent and reduces cumulative errors across related components.

questions.question: Why should related components be marked from a consistent datum?
questions.feedback: Small marking differences can accumulate, so a consistent datum helps related parts align more accurately later.

questions.question: Which item can orientation marks identify?
questions.feedback: Orientation marks help keep matching components correctly paired and facing their intended direction throughout production.

questions.question: What is one purpose of marking the waste side of a line?
options: To reduce the chance of processing the wrong side
questions.feedback: Clearly identifying the waste side helps prevent removing material from the incorrect side of a marked line.

questions.question: When should a quality gate occur?
questions.feedback: Inspection before irreversible work allows corrections while marks and component positions can still be changed.

questions.question: What should students compare at a quality gate?
options: The workshop with the production plan
questions.feedback: Comparing the component with the drawing helps confirm accuracy before permanent processing begins.

questions.question: Why is staged inspection more reliable than waiting until final assembly?
options: It prevents one early error being repeated
It removes the need for drawings
questions.feedback: Checking accuracy throughout production helps detect problems before they affect multiple related components.

questions.question: According to the theory, what should also be confirmed at a quality gate besides the drawing?
options: Orientation and relationship to matching parts
questions.feedback: Inspection should confirm orientation and matching relationships before processing makes changes difficult or impossible.

questions.question: Which practice best reduces cumulative error when marking related components?
options: Transferring measurements from one consistent datum
questions.feedback: A single consistent datum reduces the build-up of small measurement differences across multiple components.

questions.question: Where should unresolved rail, end-cap and inspection details be confirmed?
options: The teacher-issued drawing, production plan and demonstration
questions.feedback: Project-specific details come only from the approved drawing, production plan and teacher demonstration, not assumptions.

sections.title: Hole location is a design feature, not just a mark

questions.question: Why is a drilled hole treated as a designed feature?
options: Its location affects fit, alignment and function
It always improves the component's appearance
questions.feedback: Hole position influences how components fit and function, so its location must follow verified design information.

questions.question: Where should the centre position for a hole be traced from?
questions.feedback: Hole locations should always come from verified drawing information rather than estimates or copied parts.

questions.question: What should students confirm before drilling begins?
options: The correct drawing view, written information and component identity
questions.feedback: Checking the drawing view, written information and component identity helps prevent drilling the wrong feature or part.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a datum when locating a hole?
options: To provide the reference for centre locations
questions.feedback: Datums provide a consistent reference so measurements remain accurate and repeatable during marking out.

questions.question: What can happen if measurements are taken from changing edges?
options: Small errors can shift the feature
The drawing no longer needs checking
questions.feedback: Changing reference edges allow small errors to accumulate, affecting later alignment and assembly.

questions.question: Why are orientation marks important before drilling?
options: They confirm the correct face, side or end is being processed
They replace the need for a datum
questions.feedback: Orientation marks reduce the chance of drilling an accurately marked feature into the wrong component face.

questions.question: A hole intended to align with another component should remain connected to what?
questions.feedback: Understanding the design purpose helps ensure the hole is marked and checked correctly before drilling.

questions.question: Before drilling becomes irreversible, which check should be completed?
options: Compare the workpiece with the drawing, verify the datum, confirm the marked centre and check the part label
Estimate the centre position by eye
Copy the hole position from another component
questions.feedback: A complete verification confirms the feature is correctly planned before drilling permanently changes the workpiece.

questions.question: Why should students be able to explain where a hole location came from?
options: To show it was traced to verified design information
To avoid checking the marked centre
questions.feedback: Being able to explain the source shows the location was based on verified information rather than assumption.

questions.question: Why is recording the final pre-drilling check recommended?
options: It proves the hole was drilled first
It provides evidence that accuracy was planned and controlled
It replaces the need to compare with the drawing
questions.feedback: Recording the check documents that accuracy was verified before the irreversible drilling process began.

sections.title: Drill-press principles behind the teacher-issued SOP

questions.question: What does authorisation confirm before drill-press work begins?
options: The operator, workpiece and planned task are ready under required supervision
The hole location has already been drilled
The component no longer requires inspection
questions.feedback: Authorisation confirms readiness and supervision before work begins, rather than replacing the approved operating procedure.

questions.question: According to the theory, what is the main purpose of workholding?
options: To improve the appearance of the component
To prevent the component moving or rotating during drilling
To identify the correct drawing view
questions.feedback: Workholding keeps the component stable so drilling forces do not cause unwanted movement or rotation.

questions.question: Why are guarding and tool-to-work clearance considered together?
options: They replace the need for supervision
They help maintain separation from moving parts and avoid unwanted contact
questions.feedback: Guarding and suitable clearance support safe operation by preventing unintended contact with moving parts or the setup.

questions.question: What is the purpose of controlled feed during drilling?
options: To manage the cutting action instead of forcing it
questions.feedback: Controlled feed means the cutting action is managed deliberately rather than applying unnecessary force.

questions.question: Why must the operator remain aware of swarf?
options: It can affect visibility, cutting quality and inspection
It confirms the drawing is accurate
questions.feedback: Swarf can influence how well the work can be seen, assessed and cut throughout the drilling process.

questions.question: Where must the exact methods for managing drilling issues come from?
options: The current SOP and teacher demonstration
questions.feedback: The theory states that exact operating methods are controlled by the current authorised procedure and demonstration.

questions.question: How does the theory describe stopping the drill press?
options: As a deliberate stage before inspection
As the point where the drawing is selected
As an optional pause during marking out
questions.feedback: Stopping is part of the planned process and prepares the machine for safe inspection of the work and result.

questions.question: After stopping, what does inspection check?
options: Only whether the machine is clean
Whether the drilled feature matches the approved drawing and suits the next stage
Whether the operator remembers the procedure
questions.feedback: Inspection verifies both the drilled feature and the component's readiness for the following production stage.

questions.question: What does understanding drill-press principles NOT replace?
options: Authorisation, supervision and the demonstrated procedure
questions.feedback: Understanding the concepts supports safe practice but never replaces authorised procedures or required supervision.

questions.question: According to the key takeaways, what should students rely on during drill-press work?
options: The current SOP rather than memory or general knowledge
questions.feedback: Current authorised procedures take priority because they provide the approved method for the specific task being completed.

sections.title: Inspecting drilled features and responding to faults

questions.question: What is inspection mainly comparing after drilling?
options: The completed feature against the approved drawing or quality criterion
The component against similar student work
The drilling time against the production plan
questions.feedback: Inspection compares completed work with approved requirements rather than judging appearance or comparing with other components.

questions.question: Which observation best supports that a drilled feature is ready for later production stages?
options: It is suitable for later fitting or assembly
questions.feedback: Suitability for later fitting or assembly is confirmed by comparison with approved requirements, not visual similarity alone.

questions.question: Which evidence could be used during inspection according to the theory?
questions.feedback: Recorded measurements provide objective evidence that can be compared with approved drawings or quality criteria.

questions.question: A drilled feature is in the wrong location. What does this observation identify first?
questions.feedback: Fault categories describe what was observed without proving why the problem occurred.

questions.question: Before suggesting a correction, what should students do?
options: Investigate the likely cause using available evidence
questions.feedback: Evidence should be reviewed before proposing corrections because similar faults can have different causes.

questions.question: Which item may help investigate the cause of a drilling fault?
questions.feedback: Reviewing the demonstrated process can help identify likely causes without relying on unsupported assumptions.

questions.question: Why should assumptions not be presented as conclusions when investigating faults?
options: Because several causes may produce a similar fault
Because every fault has only one possible cause
Because appearance always identifies the cause
questions.feedback: Different causes can create similar outcomes, so evidence is needed before reaching conclusions.

questions.question: What should happen before any rework begins on a non-conforming feature?
options: The feature should be corrected immediately
The feature should be recorded and referred to the teacher
questions.feedback: Recording the fault and obtaining teacher review preserves evidence before any authorised rework is considered.

questions.question: Why can unauthorised correction be a problem?
options: It may remove evidence or worsen the fault
It always guarantees a better result
It automatically proves the original cause
questions.feedback: Unauthorised changes may destroy useful evidence, worsen defects or affect later production stages.

questions.question: What does careful inspection and reporting demonstrate during production?
options: Final assembly corrects all earlier faults
Appearance is more important than evidence
questions.feedback: Careful inspection shows quality was managed throughout production rather than judged only at the end.

sections.title: Reading a lathe operation through the WMS

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a lathe Work Method Statement according to the theory?
options: Connect the drawing requirement to the approved practical process
Replace the current lathe SOP during machining
questions.feedback: A WMS links the drawing, approved process and workpiece to maintain traceability throughout the operation.

questions.question: Which item should a WMS identify before machining begins?
questions.feedback: The approved setup is identified before machining so the planned process matches authorised conditions and requirements.

questions.question: Why are hold points included in a lathe WMS?
options: To check work before irreversible stages continue
questions.feedback: Hold points provide deliberate checks so early errors are identified before they affect later machining stages.

questions.question: Which information is organised into controlled stages within the WMS?
options: Planned tasks, hazards, controls, permissions and hold points
questions.feedback: Controlled stages organise essential planning information so each part of the operation can be reviewed appropriately.

questions.question: Teacher approval for continuing a task is based on what?
options: How long the task has taken
The demonstrated process, current setup and present conditions
questions.feedback: Approval depends on the demonstrated process, current setup and existing conditions rather than appearance or elapsed time.

questions.question: What should a student do if the approved setup changes during the task?
options: Continue if the drawing is unchanged
Adjust the process without reporting it
questions.feedback: Changes to approved conditions require work to stop so the WMS and authorisation can be reviewed.

questions.question: What does traceability mean in the context of the WMS?
options: Linking the drawing to the completed work through the approved process
Remembering each step without written records
Comparing one student's work with another's
questions.feedback: Traceability links the drawing, approved process and completed feature instead of relying on memory or assumptions.

questions.question: When should the WMS be reviewed?
options: When the workpiece, drawing, equipment, setup or conditions change
Only at the start of the school year
questions.feedback: The WMS should be reviewed whenever approved conditions change rather than assumed to remain automatically valid.

questions.question: Which document does a completed WMS never replace?
questions.feedback: The WMS supports planning and evidence but does not replace the current SOP or demonstrated procedures.

questions.question: According to the key takeaways, what should students do before irreversible machining stages continue?
questions.feedback: Inspection hold points help confirm the workpiece or setup before irreversible machining continues to the next stage.

sections.title: Cutting action, reference surfaces and dimensional control

questions.question: Why should material be removed progressively during lathe work?
options: To preserve shape, dimensions and surface condition
To reduce the need for drawings
To make the workpiece rotate faster
questions.feedback: Progressive removal allows controlled decisions before each change permanently affects the developing component and its accuracy.

questions.question: According to the theory, what provides a consistent basis for locating and checking features?
questions.feedback: Reference surfaces help keep later measurements and decisions connected to the same verified starting point throughout machining.

questions.question: What is the main risk of changing references without a verified reason?
options: Cumulative error and difficult measurement comparison
questions.feedback: Changing references can introduce cumulative error, making later measurements harder to compare with the approved drawing.

questions.question: Why are planned hold points included during machining?
options: To compare the developing component with verified drawing information
To make the workpiece look smoother
questions.feedback: Hold points allow deliberate checks before more material is removed, helping identify problems while correction may still be possible.

questions.question: Why are early dimensional checks more useful than finding a fault at the end?
options: They guarantee a better surface finish
Removed material cannot simply be replaced
They eliminate the need for final inspection
questions.feedback: Early checks reduce the chance of irreversible errors because removed material cannot simply be restored later.

questions.question: What should final acceptance be based on?
options: Verified measurements, the approved drawing and teacher-controlled criteria
questions.feedback: Dimensional acceptance depends on verified evidence rather than visual impressions or production speed.

questions.question: Which statement best describes machining in this theory section?
options: Cutting until the part looks correct
Removing as much material as possible
questions.feedback: Machining is presented as a controlled process where each step is guided by planned decisions and verification.

questions.question: What is the purpose of recording dimensional checks?
options: To provide evidence that quality was deliberately managed
To reduce the number of hold points
questions.feedback: Recorded checks demonstrate that quality was monitored systematically throughout machining rather than assumed afterwards.

questions.question: What does the theory say about appearance during inspection?
options: Appearance can support inspection but cannot confirm accuracy alone
questions.feedback: Visual inspection is useful, but dimensional accuracy still requires verified measurements against approved requirements.

questions.question: When checking a developing component, what should later decisions remain connected to?
options: The established datum or reference surface
questions.feedback: Maintaining the same reference surface supports consistent measurements and reduces the likelihood of cumulative error.

sections.title: Surface quality, fit and documented teacher review

questions.question: Which combination should be used to assess a machined feature?
options: Size, form, surface condition and functional fit
questions.feedback: Quality depends on considering size, form, surface condition and functional fit together rather than any single characteristic.

questions.question: Why is appearance alone not enough to judge machining quality?
options: A smooth-looking feature may still have incorrect size, form or function
Visible finish determines every quality requirement
questions.feedback: A good-looking surface does not guarantee the feature meets dimensional, form or functional requirements.

questions.question: Which inspection evidence is supported by the theory?
options: Approved measurements, observations, photographs or annotations
questions.feedback: Inspection records should use approved evidence that documents the observed quality of the machined feature.

questions.question: What should a student do if a suspected fault is found?
questions.feedback: Honest identification supports traceable quality decisions and prevents problems being concealed.

questions.question: Why should doubtful work be separated from approved components?
options: To stop it being accidentally used later
To make it easier to store
questions.feedback: Separating doubtful components reduces the risk of unsuitable work entering later production stages.

questions.question: What is required before a component is accepted or rework begins?
questions.feedback: Teacher review ensures acceptance or correction follows approved quality processes rather than assumptions.

questions.question: Why should improvised rework be avoided?
options: It may remove evidence, alter another feature or worsen the problem
questions.feedback: Unplanned rework can damage evidence or create additional faults that complicate quality assessment.

questions.question: What is the purpose of documenting the inspection result and teacher's direction?
options: To create traceable evidence of controlled quality decisions
questions.feedback: Documentation provides a record showing quality decisions were based on controlled processes rather than guesses.

questions.question: Which statement best describes functional fit?
options: Whether the feature has a shiny finish
Whether the feature can perform its intended role within the developing assembly
Whether the feature matches a photograph
questions.feedback: Functional fit considers whether the machined feature is suitable for its intended purpose in the assembly.

questions.question: According to the source boundary, where do unresolved inspection, fit and rework details come from?
options: The teacher-issued drawing, acceptance criteria, machining SOP and demonstration
questions.feedback: Project-specific inspection, fit and rework requirements are controlled by the approved documents and teacher demonstration.

sections.title: Planning plate work from verified references

questions.question: What should planning plate work begin with?
questions.feedback: Verified drawing information provides the authorised reference for identification, layout and later production decisions.

questions.question: Why are consistent datums used when marking a plate?
questions.feedback: A consistent datum keeps measurements linked to the same reference and reduces errors building across the layout.

questions.question: What is the purpose of orientation marks on a plate?
options: To show how the plate relates to surrounding components
questions.feedback: Orientation marks help maintain the correct relationship between the plate and associated components throughout production.

questions.question: Before an irreversible process begins, what should be checked?
questions.feedback: Checking marked information against the drawing helps identify errors before they become difficult or impossible to correct.

questions.question: When planning material use, what must not change?
questions.feedback: Material economy should reduce waste without changing any authorised dimensions or specifications from verified references.

questions.question: Why are planned quality hold points included during production?
options: To inspect identity, orientation, marking and condition
questions.feedback: Quality hold points provide planned opportunities to verify important production information before work continues.

questions.question: If sequencing details are unresolved, which source remains authoritative?
questions.feedback: The teacher-issued plan controls unresolved sequencing and methods, ensuring production follows the approved process.

questions.question: Which action best maintains traceability throughout production?
options: Using clear component identification and recorded checks
questions.feedback: Component identification and recorded checks link the workpiece back to verified drawing information through each stage.

questions.question: When positioning a plate within supplied stock, what should be considered?
options: Usable areas, existing edges and other components' needs
questions.feedback: Planning stock use considers available material efficiently while preserving every authorised requirement from the drawing.

questions.question: According to the theory, what should students confirm before marking or processing material?
questions.feedback: Unresolved drawing details should be confirmed first so planning and marking remain based on verified information rather than assumptions.

sections.title: Grills and guard: function, spacing and manufacturability

questions.question: Why should the grills and guard be judged together rather than as separate parts?
options: Because their function depends on consistency and alignment
Because they must always look identical
Because they are manufactured at the same time
questions.feedback: Related components should be assessed together because consistency and alignment influence their intended function and overall quality.

questions.question: According to the theory, what should spacing and alignment be checked against?
questions.feedback: Spacing and alignment should be verified against the approved drawing rather than estimated from appearance or another part.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of using consistent datums, templates or approved references?
options: To reduce repeated differences across related components
To make every component a different size
To avoid using drawings during production
questions.feedback: Consistent references reduce accumulated variation, helping related components remain aligned and function as intended.

questions.question: A student spaces grill features by eye because they look evenly arranged. What does the theory recommend instead?
options: Accept the result if it appears neat
Use verified references from the drawing
questions.feedback: Appearance alone is not sufficient because verified references provide evidence that spacing matches the approved information.

questions.question: What does manufacturability include besides producing the design accurately?
options: Considering access for processing, inspection and maintenance
questions.feedback: Manufacturability considers practical access throughout production, inspection and later maintenance, not only accurate fabrication.

questions.question: Why can repeated small variations become a problem?
options: They can affect overall fit, performance and presentation
They reduce the need for inspection
questions.feedback: Small differences can accumulate across related parts, influencing function, fit and the finished appearance.

questions.question: When should related components be compared at quality hold points?
options: Before assembly makes correction more difficult
questions.feedback: Checking related parts before assembly helps identify and correct inconsistencies while changes are still practical.

questions.question: Which evidence can demonstrate that consistency was controlled throughout production?
questions.feedback: Evidence gathered during production shows consistency was verified rather than judged only from the finished result.

questions.question: A design feature looks suitable in a sketch but blocks inspection access. According to the theory, what does this suggest?
options: The feature may be difficult to manufacture or inspect
The feature should be accepted because it looks correct
questions.feedback: Manufacturability includes practical access, so restricted inspection or processing access may make a design unsuitable.

questions.question: Where must unresolved details about grills, guards and spacing ultimately come from?
options: The teacher-issued drawings, approved quality criteria and demonstrations
questions.feedback: Project-specific spacing and manufacturing details are controlled by approved drawings, quality criteria and teacher demonstrations.

sections.title: Fit-up before permanent joining

questions.question: What is the main purpose of fit-up before permanent joining?
options: Diagnose problems while parts can still be separated
questions.feedback: Fit-up identifies issues before permanent joining, allowing components to be adjusted, repositioned or reviewed while changes remain practical.

questions.question: Which combination is specifically checked during fit-up?
options: Orientation, contact, alignment, access and assembly sequence
Paint colour, surface gloss and packaging
questions.feedback: Fit-up examines how related components work together, not unrelated workshop or presentation details.

questions.question: Why should students consider the planned assembly sequence during fit-up?
options: It may reveal that one correctly fitting part blocks later assembly
It replaces the need for approved references
questions.feedback: A component may fit individually yet prevent correct positioning or access during later assembly stages.

questions.question: What is the value of recording photographs and annotated observations during fit-up?
options: They provide evidence that component relationships were examined before joining
questions.feedback: Photographs and annotations document that fit-up checks were completed before permanent joining began.

questions.question: According to the theory, what can restraint do besides holding components together?
options: Mask poor contact or introduce movement when released
questions.feedback: Restraint can hide problems or allow movement after release, so fit-up must be evaluated carefully.

questions.question: Where heat is involved in joining, what should students understand?
options: Uneven heating and cooling may affect alignment or form
Heat removes the need for fit-up
questions.feedback: The theory explains that heating and cooling can change alignment or form and should be anticipated conceptually.

questions.question: What should happen if a mismatch or uncertainty is found during fit-up?
options: Ignore it if the assembly appears close enough
Correct it using any preferred method
questions.feedback: Problems or uncertainty should be reported before joining makes corrections more difficult or irreversible.

questions.question: Which reference should be used when reviewing fit-up?
options: Verified references including the teacher-issued drawing
questions.feedback: Fit-up decisions are checked against verified references rather than appearance or unverified examples.

questions.question: Why should permanent joining not begin simply because the assembly looks correct?
options: Appearance alone does not confirm compliance with verified references
The joining process automatically fixes errors
Inspection is only needed after joining
questions.feedback: Visual appearance alone cannot confirm correct fit, alignment or compliance with approved references.

questions.question: According to the source boundary, what controls unresolved fit-up and joining details?
options: The teacher-issued drawing, approved joining method and demonstration
questions.feedback: Project-specific fit-up and joining requirements come from the authorised drawing, method and teacher demonstration.

sections.title: Stability begins with geometry and matched components

questions.question: According to the theory, what does stable support begin with?
questions.feedback: Stable support is achieved through accurate geometry before final assembly, not by relying on later adjustment.

questions.question: Why should leg components be prepared from consistent datums?
questions.feedback: Using consistent reference points helps prevent small differences accumulating and affecting the completed assembly.

questions.question: What is the purpose of orientation marks?
options: To preserve the intended relationship between components
questions.feedback: Orientation marks help matching faces, edges or ends remain correctly related during assembly and inspection.

questions.question: Before final assembly, what should students compare against the teacher-issued drawing and approved criteria?
questions.feedback: Comparing related components against verified references helps identify problems before permanent assembly.

questions.question: If an assembly rocks, what does that symptom identify by itself?
questions.feedback: Visible symptoms alone do not identify the underlying cause and require further inspection and measurement.

questions.question: Which of the following is identified as a possible cause of misalignment?
questions.feedback: Incorrect orientation is one possible cause, alongside inconsistent references, matched-component differences and accumulated assembly error.

questions.question: What should students do first when a stability problem is observed?
options: Record the symptom and inspect the assembly
questions.feedback: Recording the symptom before inspection supports evidence-based diagnosis instead of guessing or making unnecessary changes.

questions.question: What should be used to locate the source of variation?
questions.feedback: Verified measurements provide reliable evidence for locating variation instead of relying on assumptions.

questions.question: Before making any proposed correction, what does the theory require?
questions.feedback: Teacher review helps ensure corrections are appropriate and protects component quality from unnecessary changes.

questions.question: According to the theory, stability should ultimately be achieved through what?
questions.feedback: The process demonstrates that stability comes from controlled geometry supported by measurement, inspection and review, not improvised adjustment.

sections.title: Assembly order, access and hold points

questions.question: Why is the approved assembly sequence treated as a production decision rather than just a task list?
options: It controls dependencies between components and processes
It reduces the number of components required
questions.feedback: Assembly order manages dependencies that affect access, alignment, inspection and later production stages.

questions.question: Before starting an assembly stage, what should students identify?
options: What must already be complete and what access must remain
questions.feedback: Checking prerequisites and remaining access helps prevent later assembly problems and supports controlled production.

questions.question: According to the theory, assembling a component too early may cause it to
options: Restrict later positioning, inspection or processing
questions.feedback: A correctly fitted component can still create later difficulties if it blocks access or inspection.

questions.question: Why does the theory place a quality hold point before permanent assembly continues?
options: Pause production for verified checks before continuing
Reduce the number of production stages
Replace the need for approved drawings
questions.feedback: Hold points verify important features before errors become harder to correct in later assembly.

questions.question: Which combination is checked at a quality hold point?
options: Component identity, orientation, contact, alignment and required evidence
questions.feedback: Hold points compare verified features and evidence against approved requirements before production continues.

questions.question: What risk does continuing without a hold point create?
options: An unnoticed error may affect several completed components
questions.feedback: Missing a hold point allows undetected errors to carry into later work, increasing correction effort.

questions.question: If the teacher authorises a sequence change, what should be updated?
options: The production flowchart and folio record
questions.feedback: Updating production records maintains traceability and documents the controlled change to the approved sequence.

questions.question: Why should students consider inspection and finishing before assembly proceeds?
options: To avoid using the approved sequence
Because later assembly may reduce access to important areas
To eliminate the need for drawings
questions.feedback: Some features become difficult to inspect or finish once additional components are assembled.

questions.question: What maintains traceability after a teacher-approved sequence change?
options: Recording the reason, approval and effect of the change
questions.feedback: Traceability depends on documenting why the sequence changed, who approved it and its production impact.

questions.question: Which source controls unresolved sequencing, joining, access and inspection details?
options: The teacher-issued assembly plan, drawings and demonstrations
questions.feedback: The supplied source boundary states that unresolved production details come from approved teacher documentation and demonstrations.

sections.title: Quality assurance during structural assembly

questions.question: What is the main role of quality control during structural assembly?
questions.feedback: Quality control focuses on checking results at specific stages before work progresses to the next step.

questions.question: According to the theory, quality assurance is best described as what?
options: A system showing quality was planned, checked and maintained
A method for speeding up assembly
questions.feedback: Quality assurance links planning, checking, recording and maintaining quality across the whole project, not just one inspection.

questions.question: Which combination makes inspection evidence more traceable?
options: Photographs with annotations linked to checks
questions.feedback: Traceable photographs and annotations explain what was inspected, the evidence found and any required follow-up.

questions.question: Traceable checks should connect each observation to which information?
options: The relevant component, drawing requirement, production stage and teacher-issued criterion
questions.feedback: Traceable records link observations to approved references so inspection evidence can be followed through the project.

questions.question: How should a possible failure to meet approved criteria be recorded?
options: As proof the assembly has failed completely
questions.feedback: A possible or confirmed issue should be recorded as a non-conformance rather than ignored or exaggerated.

questions.question: Before affected work continues after a possible non-conformance, what must happen?
questions.feedback: Assembly should not continue past a possible non-conformance until the teacher has reviewed the affected work.

questions.question: What should a non-conformance report avoid doing?
options: Recording that further review was needed
questions.feedback: Reports should record observed evidence without hiding issues or making unsupported claims about their cause.

questions.question: What is required before any rework begins?
questions.feedback: Rework must be authorised by the teacher before it proceeds and should then be documented.

questions.question: Which information should be included in a documented rework record?
options: The issue, approved response and later inspection result
questions.feedback: A complete rework record shows the issue, approved action and evidence from the later inspection.

questions.question: According to the theory, what does documented rework help prove?
options: Assembly quality was built through controlled decisions
Inspection records are unnecessary after rework
questions.feedback: Documented rework demonstrates that quality resulted from controlled, traceable decisions rather than appearance alone.

sections.title: Surface condition controls finish performance

questions.question: Why does finish performance begin with surface condition?
options: It determines whether the finish can bond consistently
It removes the need for inspection
questions.feedback: A clean, consistently prepared surface supports bonding, appearance and protection before the specified finish is applied.

questions.question: According to the theory, applying more finish cannot correct:
questions.feedback: Extra product cannot overcome burrs, contamination, scratches or uneven preparation that should have been addressed beforehand.

questions.question: Which stage produces the required surface condition before any finish is applied?
questions.feedback: Preparation creates the required surface condition before the specified finish is applied using the authorised method.

questions.question: A surface feels dry to the touch. What does the theory say may still be true?
options: The finish may not yet be fully cured
questions.feedback: Drying and curing are different stages, so a dry surface may still be developing its intended properties.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of planned hold-point inspections before application?
options: To identify surface issues requiring review
To confirm the finish has cured
questions.feedback: Hold-point inspections help detect burrs, contamination, inconsistent texture or damage before the finish is applied.

questions.question: Which evidence best records surface condition before application?
questions.feedback: Photographs with annotated observations provide traceable evidence that preparation was completed systematically before application.

questions.question: Which issue could reduce a finish's intended protection according to the theory?
questions.feedback: Contamination can reduce adhesion and protection, making careful preparation essential before applying the specified finish.

questions.question: What should guide every stage of preparation, application, drying and curing?
options: Current product information and teacher instructions
questions.feedback: Current product information and teacher instructions control unresolved details throughout the finishing process.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes application from preparation?
options: Application creates the required surface condition
Application places the specified finish onto the prepared surface
Application begins after curing is complete
questions.feedback: Preparation creates the surface, while application places the specified finish onto that prepared surface.

questions.question: Why should unverified substitutions or rushed handling be avoided?
options: They can affect appearance, adhesion and protection
questions.feedback: Following authorised instructions helps maintain the intended appearance, adhesion and protective performance of the finish.

sections.title: Selecting and applying a finish from authoritative information

questions.question: What should primarily justify the selection of a finish?
questions.feedback: A suitable finish is justified by confirmed performance criteria, not appearance or other unrelated preferences alone.

questions.question: Which factor is identified as one consideration when selecting a finish?
options: The number of coats previously used
questions.feedback: Future maintenance is one of several confirmed factors considered alongside protection, appearance and intended use conditions.

questions.question: Which source provides authoritative information about hazards, handling and storage?
questions.feedback: The SDS provides authoritative information about hazards, handling, storage and other controls for the product.

questions.question: Before claiming a finish is suitable, what should students do?
questions.feedback: Suitability claims should be supported by reliable product information rather than assumptions or past experience.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a product label?
options: Identify intended use and approved application requirements
Explain all hazard controls in detail
questions.feedback: The product label identifies intended use and approved application requirements, while hazard information is detailed in the SDS.

questions.question: If the planned method differs from what was approved, what should students do?
questions.feedback: Differences from the approved method require students to stop and seek clarification before continuing.

questions.question: Which combination best supports justified finish selection?
questions.feedback: Current labels, SDS and technical information provide the evidence needed to justify finish selection.

questions.question: What should folio evidence explain about the selected finish?
options: Why it was the quickest to apply
Why it meets the confirmed criteria
Why it was chosen by other students
questions.feedback: Folio evidence should explain how the specified finish satisfies the confirmed performance and maintenance criteria.

questions.question: What controls unresolved handling, application, suitability and curing details?
questions.feedback: The current teacher-specified product information and demonstration control unresolved handling, application, suitability and curing details.

questions.question: Why should current instructions be consulted and recorded in the folio?
options: To create a traceable link between planning, protection and the completed result
questions.feedback: Consulting current instructions supports traceability from production planning through material protection to the completed result.

sections.title: Finish inspection, maintenance and environmental responsibility

questions.question: What should finish inspection primarily compare the completed surface against?
questions.feedback: Inspection should compare the finish with approved criteria, producing evidence rather than relying on overall appearance.

questions.question: Which observation best supports a documented finish inspection?
options: A personal opinion about the colour
questions.feedback: Annotated observations identify what was inspected and clearly record any uncertainty needing teacher review.

questions.question: Why should students inspect edges and corners as well as larger surfaces?
options: They are less important than flat areas
They may reveal defects or inconsistent coverage
questions.feedback: Edges and corners can show defects or uneven coverage that affect comparison with approved quality criteria.

questions.question: What is the main reason a finished surface should be protected while drying and curing?
options: To prevent damage before intended properties develop
To reduce the need for inspection
questions.feedback: Protection during drying and curing helps prevent damage before the finish develops its intended properties.

questions.question: Where must the required curing conditions come from?
options: Current product information and teacher directions
questions.feedback: Curing conditions must always follow current product information together with teacher directions, not assumptions.

questions.question: When evaluating a finish, what should students consider beyond appearance?
options: Only how quickly it was applied
Maintenance, repairability and expected service life
questions.feedback: A sound evaluation considers ongoing maintenance, repairability and expected service life using confirmed information and evidence.

questions.question: Why might a finish needing frequent attention increase resource demands?
options: It may require more maintenance or earlier replacement
questions.feedback: Frequent maintenance or early replacement can increase material use and ongoing resource demands over time.

questions.question: How should leftover product and contaminated materials be managed?
options: According to teacher directions and authorised school procedures
questions.feedback: Waste management should follow authorised school procedures and teacher directions to support responsible practice.

questions.question: What provides the strongest basis for an honest finish evaluation?
options: Observed evidence supported by confirmed product information
questions.feedback: Observed evidence and confirmed product information provide a reliable basis for evaluating finish quality and performance.

questions.question: What should photographs included in finish inspection records demonstrate?
options: What was inspected and any uncertainty requiring review
questions.feedback: Inspection photographs should show inspected areas and clearly identify any uncertainty requiring teacher review.

sections.title: From three-dimensional case to flat development

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a development?
options: A flat representation of surfaces forming a three-dimensional case
A finished drawing showing the completed case only
A photograph of the assembled case
questions.feedback: A development shows how flat surfaces relate before forming, helping students understand the completed three-dimensional case.

questions.question: Why must a development be read together with the teacher-issued case drawings?
options: Because development lines may represent different features or production stages
questions.feedback: Development lines can represent different features or stages, so they must be interpreted alongside the approved case drawings.

questions.question: What is the purpose of reference lines in a development?
options: They establish where information is located and transferred
They show the finished surface appearance
questions.feedback: Reference lines organise and transfer information accurately between the development and the completed case.

questions.question: What can happen if orientation marks are not preserved?
options: A correctly shaped area may be formed in the wrong direction
The approved formulas no longer apply
questions.feedback: Orientation marks help keep faces and edges correctly related, preventing correctly shaped areas from ending up incorrectly positioned.

questions.question: According to the theory, where must allowance values come from?
options: The approved drawing, supplied formula and teacher demonstration
questions.feedback: Allowance values are controlled by approved information rather than estimates or visual guesses.

questions.question: Why are allowances included in a development?
options: To account for the material and geometry during transformation
To improve the appearance of the drawing
questions.feedback: Allowances account for how flat material changes when transformed into the required three-dimensional form.

questions.question: Why are planned hold points included in the production sequence?
options: To reduce the number of drawing views
To confirm verified information before irreversible processing
questions.feedback: Hold points provide opportunities to verify important information before later operations make correction more difficult.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the recommended way to read a development?
options: As connected surfaces that relate to the completed case
questions.feedback: A development should be interpreted as connected surfaces that together create the finished three-dimensional case.

questions.question: Why can later forming make correction more difficult?
options: Some features may no longer remain visible or accessible
Reference lines automatically disappear from the drawing
questions.feedback: Later forming can reduce access or visibility, making important checks and corrections more difficult to complete.

questions.question: According to the source boundary, who controls unresolved development, allowance, forming and sequencing details?
options: The teacher-issued drawings, approved formulas, SOPs and demonstrations
questions.feedback: The source boundary requires unresolved details to be controlled by approved documents and teacher guidance, not assumptions.

sections.title: Bending sequence, accumulated error and case fit

questions.question: Why should the teacher-issued bending sequence be followed?
options: Early bends affect later geometry, access and alignment
It guarantees no measurements are needed
questions.feedback: Following the approved sequence helps maintain geometry, access and alignment as each bend influences later forming stages.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of using consistent datums during forming?
options: To reduce accumulated error when comparing with the drawing
To increase the number of bends required
questions.feedback: Consistent datums provide stable references, reducing the chance that small differences build into larger alignment problems.

questions.question: If checks are taken from changing references, what is the most likely result?
options: Small differences may accumulate across the case
questions.feedback: Changing reference points can allow small variations to build until noticeable fit or geometry problems appear.

questions.question: According to the theory, what should be confirmed at planned hold points?
options: Orientation, reference lines, developing geometry and trial fit
questions.feedback: Hold points help identify variation early by checking orientation, references, geometry and trial fit before irreversible work continues.

questions.question: Which outcome may indicate accumulated error even when no single mistake seems large?
options: Misaligned mating edges or uneven case geometry
questions.feedback: Accumulated error often appears as overall fit or alignment problems rather than one obvious large mistake.

questions.question: What does the theory identify as springback?
options: A permanent increase in material thickness
Partial recovery towards the original shape after forming force is removed
questions.feedback: Springback describes a material's tendency to recover partly after forming, although its significance depends on the approved process.

questions.question: How should students respond to unexpected movement or accumulated error?
options: Document it and refer it to the teacher before continuing
Adjust the setup until it seems correct
Estimate a compensation value and continue
questions.feedback: Unexpected movement or mismatch should be recorded and referred rather than corrected through unapproved adjustments or guesses.

questions.question: Why are intermediate checks completed before another irreversible stage?
options: To reduce the number of drawing views
To identify where variation first appeared
To confirm the final finish quality
questions.feedback: Intermediate checks help locate the first appearance of variation before further forming makes correction more difficult.

questions.question: What should students avoid doing when springback is suspected?
questions.feedback: The theory states that compensation values must not be guessed because relevance depends on the confirmed material and approved process.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the relationship between each bend and the developing case?
options: Each bend can influence later features and references
Each bend is independent of later stages
Only the final bend affects case fit
questions.feedback: Each forming stage influences later geometry, reference points and alignment, making the approved sequence important throughout the process.

sections.title: Hinges and handle as an evidence-based design problem

questions.question: What should students do before generating hinge and handle arrangements?
questions.feedback: Confirmed constraints from authorised sources establish what the design must resolve before alternatives are generated.

questions.question: How should an unverified assumption about the arrangement be treated?
questions.feedback: Unverified assumptions should remain recorded questions until confirmed through teacher-issued information or authorised review.

questions.question: Why should students generate several possible arrangements?
questions.feedback: Generating alternatives allows students to evaluate different solutions against approved functional and manufacturing criteria.

questions.question: Which set contains only approved comparison criteria named in the theory?
questions.feedback: Movement, access and ergonomics are identified criteria for comparing how effectively each arrangement may function.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a comparison table or annotated sketches?
options: To prove the arrangement is safe
questions.feedback: Tables, sketches and design notes show how alternatives were compared and why one may be preferred.

questions.question: When authorised, why can a prototype provide stronger evidence than appearance alone?
options: It removes the need for approval
questions.feedback: A prototype may expose restricted movement, poor access, awkward handling or manufacturing problems hidden in sketches.

questions.question: What should students record after an approved trial fit?
options: Only evidence supporting their preferred design
A claim that the design is complete
questions.feedback: Honest documentation must include trial results, identified problems and any questions that remain unresolved.

questions.question: Which evidence best supports selecting a final arrangement?
questions.feedback: Selection should be justified through approved comparison criteria and evidence gathered from any authorised testing.

questions.question: When may an arrangement be described as safe, suitable or complete?
options: After teacher review and required testing
questions.feedback: Such claims require teacher review and completion of the required testing, not student judgement alone.

questions.question: What does recording alternatives, evidence and approval points demonstrate?
questions.feedback: These records demonstrate that the final decision developed systematically through comparison, testing and authorised approval.

sections.title: PMI evaluation that moves beyond opinion

questions.question: What should a PMI evaluation judge the completed BBQ and case against?
options: The teacher-issued brief and approved criteria
questions.feedback: A PMI evaluation is evidence-based and compares the project with the approved expectations rather than personal opinion.

questions.question: According to the theory, what should support every Plus observation?
options: Evidence such as photographs, measurements, testing records or folio notes
questions.feedback: A Plus is strengthened by evidence that demonstrates the successful feature or process outcome being described.

questions.question: When writing a Minus observation, what should students describe before suggesting a likely cause?
questions.feedback: Describing the effect first separates observed evidence from later explanations about why the issue may have occurred.

questions.question: When should a cause be presented as confirmed?
options: Only when supported by available evidence
questions.feedback: The theory requires causes to remain tentative unless evidence is sufficient to support the conclusion.

questions.question: Which statement best describes an Interesting observation?
options: It identifies a meaningful result or relationship worth further consideration
It is another compliment about the finished project
It lists personal likes about the design
questions.feedback: Interesting observations extend evaluation by exploring meaningful findings rather than repeating praise or opinions.

questions.question: A production decision unexpectedly influenced both quality and the relationship between the BBQ and its case. Which PMI category best fits this finding?
questions.feedback: Unexpected relationships between production decisions and outcomes are identified as Interesting observations in the PMI.

questions.question: What should conclude a strong PMI evaluation?
options: One achievable improvement based on evidence
questions.feedback: The final improvement should respond to evidence, address a likely cause and remain realistic within project constraints.

questions.question: Which approach best follows the PMI process?
options: Link each observation to approved criteria and evidence
Record only personal likes and dislikes
questions.feedback: PMI observations gain credibility when they are clearly connected to approved criteria and supporting evidence.

questions.question: Why should proposed improvements be realistic within available processes and project constraints?
options: So the recommendation can realistically be applied
questions.feedback: Useful improvements are achievable and grounded in the project's available processes, evidence and constraints.

questions.question: According to the source boundary, what controls unresolved judgements, results and improvement claims?
options: The teacher-issued brief, approved criteria and completed project evidence
questions.feedback: Where uncertainty remains, the brief, approved criteria and completed project evidence determine justified evaluation claims.

sections.title: Building the project report as an evidence chain

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the project report?
options: Form an evidence chain from brief to evaluation
questions.feedback: The report should connect decisions, production evidence and evaluation into a traceable sequence rather than disconnected documents.

questions.question: Which item should begin the evidence chain?
questions.feedback: The evidence chain starts with the approved brief before later planning, production and evaluation evidence is presented.

questions.question: Why should production photographs be arranged chronologically?
options: To reduce the number of images
To show stages, hold points, problems and authorised responses in sequence
questions.feedback: Chronological order helps readers follow how production progressed and how important decisions affected outcomes.

questions.question: What should every production photograph include?
options: A concise caption explaining its purpose
questions.feedback: Captions should identify what is shown, why it matters and which requirement or decision the evidence supports.

questions.question: If the completed project differs from the original plan, what should the report do?
options: Record the as-built result and acknowledge the change
Replace the original plan with a new version
questions.feedback: An accurate report records what was actually made and openly acknowledges changes from earlier planning.

questions.question: Which sources should be identified when they informed decisions?
options: Teacher-issued drawings, product information and demonstrations
questions.feedback: Identifying sources shows where important production decisions were informed by authoritative information.

questions.question: What should you do if evidence is missing?
options: Do not invent it or recreate it inaccurately
questions.feedback: Missing evidence must remain honest rather than being invented or reconstructed inaccurately.
